In [[geometry]], the '''orthocentroidal circle''' of a non-equilateral [[triangle]] is the circle that has the triangle's [[orthocenter]] and [[centroid]] at opposite ends of its [[diameter]]. This diameter also contains the triangle's [[nine-point center]] and is a subset of the [[Euler line]], which also contains the [[circumcenter]] outside the orthocentroidal circle.

[[Andrew Guinand]] showed in 1984 that the triangle's [[incenter]] must lie in the interior of the orthocentroidal circle, but not coinciding with the nine-point center; that is, it must fall in the open '''orthocentroidal disk''' punctured at the nine-point center.<ref>{{citation|first=Andrew P.|last=Guinand|title=Euler lines, tritangent centers, and their triangles|journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]]|volume=91|issue=5|jstor=2322671|year=1984|pages=290–300|doi=10.2307/2322671}}.</ref><ref name=Bradley>{{citation|first1=Christopher J.|last1=Bradley|first2=Geoff C.|last2=Smith|title=The locations of triangle centers|journal=[[Forum Geometricorum]]|volume=6|year=2006|pages=57–70|url=http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2006volume6/FG200607index.html|access-date=2014-11-04|archive-date=2016-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304000426/http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2006volume6/FG200607index.html|url-status=dead}}.</ref><ref name=Stern>{{citation
 | last = Stern
 | first = Joseph
 | journal = [[Forum Geometricorum]]
 | pages = 1–9
 | title = Euler's triangle determination problem
 | url = http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2007volume7/FG200701.pdf

 | access-date = 2014-11-04

 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20211026093158/http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2007volume7/FG200701.pdf
 | url-status = dead
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation|last=Franzsen|first=William N.|title=The distance from the incenter to the Euler line|journal=[[Forum Geometricorum]]|volume=11|year=2011|pages=231–236|url=http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2011volume11/FG201126index.html}}.</ref>

The incenter could be any such point, depending on the specific triangle having that particular orthocentroidal disk.<ref name=Stern/>

Furthermore,<ref name=Bradley/> the [[Fermat point]], the [[Gergonne point]], and the [[symmedian point]] are in the open orthocentroidal disk punctured at its own center (and could be at any point therein), while the [[Fermat point#Aliases|second Fermat point]] and [[Feuerbach point]] are in the exterior of the orthocentroidal circle. The [[locus (mathematics)|set of potential locations]] of one or the other of the [[Brocard points]] is also the open orthocentroidal disk.<ref>{{citation|first1=Christopher J.|last1=Bradley|first2=Geoff C.|last2=Smith|title=The locations of the Brocard points|journal=[[Forum Geometricorum]]|volume=6|year=2006|pages=71–77|url=http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2006volume6/FG200608index.html|access-date=2014-11-05|archive-date=2016-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304000144/http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2006volume6/FG200608index.html|url-status=dead}}.</ref>

The square of the diameter of the orthocentroidal circle is<ref name="ac">Altshiller-Court, Nathan, ''College Geometry'', Dover Publications, 2007 (orig. Barnes & Noble 1952).</ref>{{rp|p.102}}  <math>D^2-\tfrac{4}{9}(a^2+b^2+c^2),</math> where ''a, b,'' and ''c'' are the triangle's side lengths and ''D'' is the diameter of its [[circumcircle]].

The orthocentroidal circle, circumcircle, [[nine-point circle]], [[Polar circle (geometry)|polar circle]] and circumcircle of the [[tangential triangle]] are [[Coaxal circles|coaxal]], and all meet on the common radical axis if the triangle is not acute. The radical axis is the [[orthic axis]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Coaxal System |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/CoaxalSystem.html |website=MathWorld--A Wolfram Web Resource. |publisher=Wolfram Research |access-date=27 November 2025 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kimberling |first=Clark |title=P(4) 1st GRINBERG INTERSECTION |url=https://faculty.evansville.edu/ck6/encyclopedia/BicentricPairs.html#P4 |access-date=25 June 2025 |website=Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers}}</ref>
